paras: The killing of Sampson Hunter was the shooting of a Black man by James Orso, a white justice of the peace, who came with three men to arrest him at Escatawpa, Washington County, Alabama, on the night of February 12, 1881. Hunter resisted with an ax, was shot, and died the next morning. A jury of inquiry heard the evidence, and Orso was reported at home awaiting arrest.

According to inquiry testimony, Orso and Hunter came to blows at about 8 p.m., Hunter supposedly striking Orso with an ax handle. After the two were separated, Hunter went home to a shanty owned by E. Garrettson, for whom he worked.

At nine o'clock Orso came to arrest Hunter for a breach of the peace, accompanied by Cessford, Malono and O'Denell. Garrettson, who came to quiet the matter, was knocked senseless by an unknown hand. When Hunter refused to surrender, the party rushed in, and he fought back with a turpentine ax.

Orso fired a double-barreled shotgun, breaking Hunter's right arm and lodging a ball in his right breast. In the party's account, Hunter would have killed Orso had Cessford not knocked him down. Hunter lived until 7 a.m. on Sunday.
W. T. Miller recorded the evidence before a jury of inquiry, whose finding does not appear in the coverage. Orso was said to be at home awaiting arrest; no report of an arrest or trial was found.

The earliest report was a Mobile wire in the Omaha Daily Bee on February 16, headlined "Captured His Man." It named the victim both "Sampson Daker" and "Hunter" and said he died in a few minutes. On February 23 the Alexandria Gazette gave the fullest version, from a Mississippi paper, the Messenger, as "Fearful Tragedy." The Jackson Comet followed on February 26 with a Mobile "Special to the Democrat" headed "A Desperate Fight in Washington County Alabama."
Every account came from the arresting party's side, and none of the papers questioned the shooting.
The inquiry-based account dated the fight Saturday the 12th, consistent with the Comet's February 14 dispatch, while the Bee's February 16 wire said "last night."

reader.title: Killing of Sampson Hunter
bases: A justice of the peace and three men went to arrest Hunter for a breach of the peace and the justice shot him when he resisted with an ax (A1, A2, A3).

Hunter was killed by a party of four led by a justice of the peace acting to arrest him for a breach of the peace, and the papers describe a resisted arrest rather than a group acting to punish or kill him (A2, A3); whether the killing was lawful is not settled in the coverage, which reports a jury of inquiry and Orso awaiting arrest but no outcome (A2, A3).
A Mobile wire, a Mobile special to the Democrat and a Mississippi paper's account drawn from inquiry testimony agree that Orso shot Hunter while trying to arrest him (A1, A2, A3).

accounts.label: Mobile wire
accounts.gist: After a fight, Orzo, a justice of the peace, and three men tried to arrest Hunter, who resisted with an axe and was shot in the breast, dying within minutes.

accounts.label: Evidence before the jury of inquiry (via a Mississippi Messenger)
accounts.gist: Orso went at nine with three men to arrest Hunter for a breach of the peace; Hunter fought with a turpentine ax, was shot, knocked down by Cessford, and died at 7 a.m. Sunday.

accounts.label: Mobile special to the Democrat
accounts.gist: Orso, with a posse and Garretson, went to arrest Hunter, who would have killed Orso with the ax had one of the crowd not knocked him off; Orso is awaiting arrest.

framing.detail: The Bee ran the Mobile wire under 'Captured His Man', presenting the shooting as an arrest.
The Gazette's 'Fearful Tragedy' gave the inquiry testimony in detail, with Hunter's 'very vigorous resistance'.
The Comet's 'A Desperate Fight' called it 'a fearful tragedy' and stressed that Hunter would have killed Orso.

versions.value: before a Mobile dispatch of Feb. 14 ('that night')
'last night' in a dispatch of Feb. 16

conflicts.note: The inquiry-based account is the most detailed and fits the Feb. 14 dateline; the Bee's 'last night' looks like a delayed wire.
The inquiry evidence is the better source.
The Bee's 'Daker' appears to be an error within one sentence that also calls him Hunter.
